sections.title: Word Order Is SOV
sections.rule: Korean sentences follow Subject–Object–Verb order, and the verb or adjective must come at the very end of the clause. Everything else (time, place, object) is arranged before the predicate.
sections.example_ref: English: I eat an apple. / I go to school.
sections.note: Romanization: naneun sagwareul meogeoyo. Because the verb is always last, listen to the end of a sentence to catch tense and negation.

sections.title: Topic 은/는 vs Subject 이/가
sections.rule: 은/는 marks the topic or sets up contrast ('as for…'); 이/가 marks the grammatical subject, often new or emphasized information. Use 은/받침 없음→는, 이/받침 있음→가 based on whether the noun ends in a consonant.
sections.example_ref: English: As for me, I'm a student. / Who came? A friend came.
sections.note: Romanization: jeoneun haksaengieyo. Answering 'who/what' uses 이/가; introducing a topic uses 은/는.

sections.title: Object 을/를 and Place 에/에서
sections.rule: 을/를 marks the direct object (을 after a consonant, 를 after a vowel). 에 marks a static location, direction, or time; 에서 marks the place where an action happens or a starting point ('from').
sections.example_ref: English: I read a book at the library. / I am at home.
sections.note: Romanization: doseogwaneseo chaegeul ilgeoyo. 있다/살다 take 에 (existence); action verbs take 에서.

sections.title: Polite Endings 아/어요 and 습니다
sections.rule: -아/어요 is the everyday polite style used in most conversation; -습니다/ㅂ니다 is the formal polite style for news, presentations, and the military. Both are polite, but 습니다 is more distant and official.
sections.example_ref: English: Where are you going? / I live in Seoul.
sections.note: Romanization: eodie gayo? Add -ㅂ니다 after a vowel stem (갑니다) and -습니다 after a consonant stem (먹습니다).

sections.title: Past, Present, and Future
sections.rule: Present/habitual uses -아/어요 (먹어요, eat). Past inserts -았/었- before 어요 (먹었어요, ate). Future intention uses -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (먹을 거예요, will eat).
sections.example_ref: English: I watched a movie yesterday. / I will meet a friend tomorrow.
sections.note: Romanization: eoje yeonghwareul bwasseoyo. Vowel harmony: stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take 았/아, all others take 었/어.

sections.title: Negation: 안 and 지 않아요
sections.rule: Place 안 directly before the verb (안 먹어요, don't eat) or attach -지 않아요 to the stem (먹지 않아요). Both mean the same; -지 않아요 is slightly more formal. 하다 verbs split: 공부 안 해요.
sections.example_ref: English: I don't drink coffee. / I'm not working today.
sections.note: Romanization: jeoneun keopireul an masyeoyo. For 있다/알다 use the opposite words 없다/모르다, not 안.

sections.title: Descriptive Verbs (Adjectives)
sections.rule: Korean adjectives are 'descriptive verbs' that conjugate like action verbs and end the sentence, so no separate 'to be' is needed. 크다 (to be big) → 커요 (is big); 작다 → 작아요.
sections.example_ref: English: The weather is good. / This bag is expensive.
sections.note: Romanization: nalssiga joayo. To modify a noun, an adjective takes -(으)ㄴ: 예쁜 꽃 (a pretty flower).

sections.title: The Honorific Infix 시
sections.rule: Insert -(으)시- into the verb when the subject deserves respect (elders, teachers, customers). 가다 → 가세요; 읽다 → 읽으세요. It raises the subject, not the listener.
sections.example_ref: English: Grandmother is sleeping. / The teacher is coming now.
sections.note: Romanization: halmeonikkeseo jumuseyo. The subject often takes honorific 께서 instead of 이/가, and some verbs are irregular (자다→주무시다).

sections.title: Connective Endings 고, 어서, 지만
sections.rule: -고 links two clauses ('and/then'); -아/어서 shows cause or sequence ('so/because'); -지만 shows contrast ('but'). They attach to the verb stem and let one sentence carry several clauses.
sections.example_ref: English: I was hungry so I ate. / It's expensive but delicious.
sections.note: Romanization: baega gopaseo babeul meogeosseoyo. With -아/어서 you cannot put a past-tense marker on the first clause; tense goes only on the final verb.

sections.title: Ability 수 있다 and Desire 고 싶다
sections.rule: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 expresses can/cannot (할 수 있어요, I can do it). -고 싶다 expresses 'want to' with a verb (가고 싶어요, I want to go).
sections.example_ref: English: I can speak Korean. / I want to eat bulgogi.
sections.note: Romanization: jeoneun hangugeoreul hal su isseoyo. For 'want a noun' use 이/가 + 싶다? No—use 을/를 갖고 싶다; 고 싶다 attaches only to verbs.

sections.title: Counters and Two Number Systems
sections.rule: Native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋…) combine with counters like 명 (people), 개 (things), 마리 (animals); before a counter 하나→한, 둘→두. Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼…) are used for dates, money, minutes, and phone numbers.
sections.example_ref: English: Two coffees, please. / It's now 3:30.
sections.note: Romanization: keopi du jan juseyo. Hours use native numbers (세 시) but minutes use Sino numbers (삼십 분).

sections.title: Honorific and Humble Vocabulary
sections.rule: Certain everyday words have special respectful forms for elders: 먹다→드시다/잡수시다, 자다→주무시다, 있다→계시다. To lower yourself, use humble words: 나→저, 주다→드리다.
sections.example_ref: English: Father is eating (his meal). / I will help you (humbly).
sections.note: Romanization: abeojikkeseo jinjireul japsuseyo. Raise the other person with honorific words; lower yourself with humble words — never mix them up.

sections.title: Irregular Verb Stems
sections.rule: Some stems change before endings: ㅂ→우 (덥다→더워요), ㄷ→ㄹ (듣다→들어요), 르→ㄹㄹ (모르다→몰라요), ㅅ drops (짓다→지어요), ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다→살아요, 삽니다).
sections.example_ref: English: The weather is very hot today. / I don't know that person.
sections.note: Romanization: oneureun nalssiga neomu deowoyo. Not every ㅂ/ㄷ stem is irregular (잡다→잡아요 is regular) — memorize which ones change.

sections.title: Quoting and Reported Speech
sections.rule: Report statements with -다고 하다 (verbs) or -(이)라고 하다 (nouns). Questions use -냐고, commands -(으)라고, suggestions -자고. The quoted clause keeps its own tense.
sections.example_ref: English: My friend said he would come tomorrow. / He said he is a student.
sections.note: Romanization: chinguga naeil ondago haesseoyo. In casual speech -다고 하다 often contracts to -대요 (온대요, they say he's coming).

sections.title: Conditional Ending 으면
sections.rule: Attach -(으)면 to a verb or adjective stem to mean 'if' or 'when'. -면 follows a vowel stem, -으면 follows a consonant stem. The result clause comes after.
sections.example_ref: English: If I have time, let's meet. / If it rains, I won't go.
sections.note: Romanization: sigani isseumyeon mannayo. For a strong hypothetical add 만약: 만약 제가 부자라면 (if I were rich).

sections.title: Intention 려고 and Purpose 러
sections.rule: -(으)려고 (하다) expresses intention or plan ('intend to'); -(으)러 expresses the purpose of going/coming and pairs with movement verbs 가다/오다. Both attach to a verb stem.
sections.example_ref: English: I intend to study abroad next year. / I go to the restaurant to eat.
sections.note: Romanization: naenyeone yuhak garyeogo haeyo. Use -러 only with come/go verbs; for other purposes use -(으)려고 or -기 위해.

sections.title: Obligation and Permission
sections.rule: -아/어야 되다/하다 means 'must/have to' (가야 돼요). -아/어도 되다 gives permission 'may' (먹어도 돼요). -(으)면 안 되다 forbids 'must not' (들어가면 안 돼요).
sections.example_ref: English: I have to go home now. / May I sit here?
sections.note: Romanization: jigeum jibe gaya dwaeyo. 되다 and 하다 are interchangeable after -아/어야; 돼요 is more conversational.

sections.title: Prohibition Command 지 마세요
sections.rule: Attach -지 마세요 to a verb stem to tell someone politely not to do something; the plain form is -지 마 and the very formal form is -지 마십시오.
sections.example_ref: English: Please don't smoke here. / Don't worry too much.
sections.note: Romanization: yeogieseo dambaereul piuji maseyo. 마세요 comes from 말다 (to stop/quit), which is itself irregular (말 + 세요).

sections.title: Doing a Favor 아/어 주다
sections.rule: -아/어 주다 means doing an action for someone's benefit. Use 주세요 to request a favor politely, and 주시겠어요? for extra politeness; 드리다 is the humble form when you do it for a senior.
sections.example_ref: English: Please take a photo (for me). / My friend bought the ticket for me.
sections.note: Romanization: sajin jom jjigeo juseyo. Add 좀 to soften a request; use 드리다 instead of 주다 when helping someone older.

sections.title: Nominalization 는 것 and 기
sections.rule: Turn a verb into a noun with -는 것 (the act of / the fact that) or -기. -는 것을 좋아하다 = 'like doing'; -기 is common with adjectives of difficulty/ease and set phrases.
sections.example_ref: English: I like exercising. / Learning Korean is fun.
sections.note: Romanization: jeoneun undonghaneun geoseul joahaeyo. -는 것 often contracts to -는 게 in speech (운동하는 게 좋아요).

sections.title: Noun-Modifying (Relative) Endings
sections.rule: Korean relative clauses come before the noun. With action verbs: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는, future -(으)ㄹ. With adjectives, the present modifier is -(으)ㄴ. Word order is [clause] + noun.
sections.example_target_2: 저기 앉아 있는 사람이 제 동생이에요.
sections.example_ref: English: The book I bought yesterday is interesting. / The person sitting over there is my younger sibling.
sections.note: Romanization: eoje san chaegi jaemiisseoyo. Adjectives use -(으)ㄴ for the present (예쁜 꽃), while verbs use -는 for the present (사는 사람).

sections.title: Conjecture 을 것 같다
sections.rule: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 expresses a guess or impression ('seems / probably will'). Use -는 것 같다 for a present action, -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 for a past guess, and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 for a future guess.
sections.example_ref: English: It looks like it will rain today. / This food looks like it will be delicious.
sections.note: Romanization: oneul biga ol geot gatayo. 것 같다 softens statements, so Koreans use it to sound less blunt even when fairly sure.
